content: Sucrose has been studied for its potential to provide calming and analgesic effects in neonates undergoing invasive procedures, such as heel lances. The objective of this research was to evaluate the effectiveness of sucrose in alleviating pain during these procedures, considering both immediate and long-term outcomes. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases and trial registries up to February 2022. Randomized controlled trials involving term and/or preterm neonates who received sucrose for heel lances were included. Comparisons were made with interventions such as water, placebo, non-nutritive sucking (NNS), glucose, breastfeeding, breast milk, music, acupuncture, facilitated tucking, and skin-to-skin care. Standard Cochrane methods were employed for data collection and analysis, and the certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The analysis included 55 trials involving 6,273 neonates. Among these, 29 trials focused on term neonates, 22 on preterm neonates, and 4 on both groups. Heel lance procedures were the primary focus in 50 trials, while 15 trials also investigated other minor painful procedures. 1. Sucrose vs. Control (Water/Placebo/No Intervention): Sucrose likely reduces pain as measured by the Premature Infant Pain Profile (PIPP) scores at 30 seconds (mean difference [MD] -1.74, 95% confidence interval [CI] -2.11 to -1.37) and 60 seconds (MD -2.14, 95% CI -3.34 to -0.94) after lancing. This evidence is of moderate certainty. The effect of sucrose on the DAN (Douleur Aiguë du Nouveau-né) scores compared to water at 30 seconds is very uncertain (MD -1.90, 95% CI -8.58 to 4.78; very low-certainty evidence). Sucrose likely reduces Neonatal Infant Pain Scale (NIPS) scores immediately after lancing (MD -2.00, 95% CI -2.42 to -1.58; moderate-certainty evidence). 2. Sucrose vs. Non-Nutritive Sucking (NNS): The effect of sucrose on PIPP scores during the recovery period after lancing is very uncertain (MD 0.60, 95% CI -0.30 to 1.50; very low-certainty evidence). The effect of sucrose on DAN scores at 30 seconds after lancing is also very uncertain (MD -1.20, 95% CI -7.87 to 5.47; very low-certainty evidence). 3. Sucrose + NNS vs. NNS Alone: The combination of sucrose and NNS may reduce PIPP scores during lancing (MD -4.90, 95% CI -5.73 to -4.07) and during recovery (MD -3.80, 95% CI -4.47 to -3.13), but the evidence is very uncertain (very low-certainty evidence). The effect of sucrose + NNS on Neonatal Facial Coding System (NFCS) scores compared to water + NNS during lancing is very uncertain (MD -0.60, 95% CI -1.47 to 0.27; very low-certainty evidence). 4. Sucrose vs. Glucose: Sucrose appears to have little to no difference in PIPP scores compared to glucose at 30 seconds (MD 0.26, 95% CI -0.70 to 1.22) and 60 seconds (MD -0.02, 95% CI -0.79 to 0.75) after lancing. This evidence is of low certainty. 5. Sucrose vs. Breastfeeding: The effect of sucrose on PIPP scores compared to breastfeeding at 30 seconds after lancing is very uncertain (MD -0.70, 95% CI -0.49 to 1.88; very low-certainty evidence). The effect of sucrose on COMFORTneo scores compared to breastfeeding after lancing is also very uncertain (MD -2.60, 95% CI -3.06 to -2.14; very low-certainty evidence). 6. Sucrose vs. Expressed Breast Milk: Sucrose may result in little to no difference in PIPP-R scores compared to expressed breast milk during lancing (MD 0.3, 95% CI -0.24 to 0.84) and at 30 seconds after lancing (MD 0.3, 95% CI -0.11 to 0.71). This evidence is of low certainty. Sucrose may slightly increase PIPP-R scores compared to expressed breast milk at 60 seconds after lancing (MD 1.10, 95% CI 0.34 to 1.86; low-certainty evidence). The effect of sucrose on DAN scores compared to expressed breast milk at 30 seconds after lancing is very uncertain (MD -1.80, 95% CI -8.47 to 4.87; very low-certainty evidence). 7. Sucrose vs. Laser Acupuncture: The effect of sucrose on NIPS scores compared to laser acupuncture during lancing is very uncertain (MD -0.86, 95% CI -1.43 to -0.29; very low-certainty evidence). 8. Sucrose vs. Facilitated Tucking: The effect of sucrose on total Behavioral Pain Scale for Neonates (BPSN) scores compared to facilitated tucking during lancing (MD -2.27, 95% CI -4.66 to 0.12) and during recovery (MD -0.31, 95% CI -1.72 to 1.10) is very uncertain (very low-certainty evidence). 9. Sucrose vs. Skin-to-Skin Care + Water (Repeated Lancing): Sucrose appears to result in little to no difference in PIPP scores compared to skin-to-skin care + water at 30 seconds after the first (MD 0.13, 95% CI -0.70 to 0.96), second (MD -0.56, 95% CI -1.57 to 0.45), or third lancing (MD -0.15, 95% CI -1.26 to 0.96). This evidence is of low certainty. Similarly, sucrose results in little to no difference in PIPP scores at 60 seconds after the first (MD -0.61, 95% CI -1.55 to 0.33), second (MD -0.12, 95% CI -0.99 to 0.75), or third lancing (MD -0.40, 95% CI -1.48 to 0.68). This evidence is also of low certainty. Minor adverse events associated with sucrose administration were reported but required no intervention. In conclusion, sucrose likely reduces pain as measured by PIPP scores at 30 and 60 seconds after single heel lances compared to control interventions (moderate-certainty evidence). However, the evidence is very uncertain regarding its effects compared to NNS, breastfeeding, laser acupuncture, facilitated tucking, or sucrose combined with NNS. Sucrose appears to have little to no difference in pain scores compared to glucose, expressed breast milk, or skin-to-skin care. The use of sucrose in combination with other non-pharmacologic interventions should be approached with caution due to the uncertainty of the evidence.
